Here are verse-by-verse notes on 2 Samuel 9, drawn from the sources accessible via the searches and fetches above.

---

## 2 Samuel 9 — Overview

The chapter is widely regarded across traditions as one of the most beautiful pictures of grace in the Old Testament. Dr. Thomas Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary, evangelical) calls it "the greatest illustration of grace in all the Old Testament" (quoting Swindoll). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]

The Hebrew word *hesed* (lovingkindness, loyal covenant love) appears three times in this chapter (vv. 1, 3, 7) and is the key theological term. Ligonier (Reformed) explains: "*Hesed* refers to enduring covenant love, the kind of love that seeks the good of the covenant partner and does not break its promises." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mephibosheth-sits-at-kings-table]

Precept Austin (evangelical) notes that while the word "covenant" does not appear in the chapter, the story is "one of the most beautiful illustrations of the solemn and binding nature of covenant in all of Scripture." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary]

---

### v. 1 — "Then David asked, 'Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?'"

**Traditional reading (Evangelical / older commentaries):**

- **Timing:** The Pulpit Commentary estimates the events occurred about 17–18 years after the battle of Gilboa, when David had been king over all Israel for about nine years. Mephibosheth was five when Saul and Jonathan died (2 Sam. 4:4); now he has a son of his own (v. 12), so sufficient time had passed. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **David's initiative:** Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic) stresses that David initiated the search — the person needing mercy was not seeking the king. "How like our Great God Who sought us and bought us with the price of blood when we were lame, unlovely and uninterested in Him!" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

- **Covenant motivation:** David acted because of his covenant with Jonathan (1 Sam. 20:14–17). Gill notes that David did this "not for Saul's sake, who had been his implacable enemy… but for Jonathan's sake, his dear friend, whose memory was precious to him." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Contrast with worldly politics:** Precept Austin quotes Ralph Davis: "According to the wisdom of the age such promises would be regarded as the height or depth of folly. When a new regime or dynasty came to power, the name of the game was purge." David did the opposite. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary]

- **"For Jonathan's sake" as typology:** Spurgeon (Baptist) draws a direct parallel to the Gospel: "Like Mephibosheth, we may cry unto the King of Glory, 'What is thy servant, that thou shouldst look upon such a dead dog as I am?' but still the Lord indulges us with most familiar intercourse with Himself, because He sees in our countenances the remembrance of His dearly-beloved Jesus." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary] and [https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/morneve/morneve.d0527am.html]

**Reformed reading (Ligonier):** Hesed is more than sentiment — "it bears fruit in tangible action." David's search shows that covenant love takes initiative. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mephibosheth-sits-at-kings-table]

---

### v. 2 — "And there was a servant of Saul’s family named Ziba. They summoned him to David, and the king inquired, 'Are you Ziba?' 'I am your servant,' he replied."

- **Ziba's role:** The Pulpit Commentary suggests Ziba had probably been steward over Saul's property in Benjamin and had continued in possession of it after Saul's death. David had not interfered with it. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Ziba's later treachery:** Precept Austin notes that while Ziba appears cooperative here, later events (2 Sam. 16:1–4; 19:24–30) reveal him as "a self-seeking conniving scoundrel" who lied about Mephibosheth to gain his property. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary]

- Gill notes the Jewish tradition that Ziba was a Canaanite servant who, upon Saul's death, became the inheritance of his children (Lev. 25:46), though Josephus says he was freed by Saul. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/9.htm]

---

### v. 3 — "So the king asked, 'Is there anyone left of Saul’s family to whom I can show the kindness of God?' Ziba answered, 'There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.'"

- **"The kindness of God":** The Pulpit Commentary explains this is a Hebrew idiom meaning "extraordinary kindness" — the devout Orientals "saw in everything that was more than common a manifestation of God, and thus the epithet 'of God' came to be applied to anything that was very great." David wanted to show kindness as wonderful as God's dealings with man. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Ellicott similarly says: "kindness such as God shows, very great, and in the fear of God." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Ziba's emphasis on the lameness:** Precept Austin observes that Ziba does not even name Mephibosheth but focuses on his physical deformity — yet David does not respond, "Isn't there someone else who is not lame?" David looked past the outward appearance. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary]

- **David's question uses "the King" title:** Precept Austin notes the narrator refers to David as "the King" when addressing Ziba (vv. 2, 3, 4, 9), but as "David" when addressing Mephibosheth (vv. 6, 7), suggesting a personal versus official relationship. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary]

- Dr. Constable suggests the repeated mention of Mephibosheth's lameness (vv. 3, 13) may remind readers "of the sad fate of Saul's line because of his arrogance before God." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]

---

### v. 4 — "'Where is he?' replied the king. And Ziba said, 'Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.'"

- **Lo-debar:** The name literally means "no pasture," suggesting a barren, desolate place. Enduring Word says this speaks of Mephibosheth's "low station in life — he didn't even have his own house." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

- Dr. Constable locates it "about 10 miles northwest of Jabesh-gilead in Transjordan and 10 miles south of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee)." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]

- **Machir son of Ammiel:** Ellicott notes that from 2 Sam. 17:27–29, Machir appears as a man of wealth and position. He was probably "secretly an adherent to the house of Saul" until David's kindness won his heart, after which he became a faithful friend to David during Absalom's rebellion. Ellicott also speculates whether Ammiel is the same as in 1 Chron. 3:5 (called Eliam in 2 Sam. 11:3), which would make Machir the brother of Bathsheba, but acknowledges the name was common. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Dr. Constable says it is "doubtful" that Ammiel was Bathsheba's father. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]

- The Pulpit Commentary suggests Machir may have been won over by the magnanimity of David's actions: "There was a magnanimity about it which would commend it to a man who was himself generous and true." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

---

### v. 5 — "So King David had him brought from the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar."

- **David "fetched" him (KJV):** Enduring Word comments that David did not merely send a message telling Mephibosheth to pick up his crutches and make his own way. "David made a way for him and provided the means for him to come." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

- Mephibosheth must have been terrified. Enduring Word says: "In the back of his mind, he anticipated the day when David would do as other kings did and massacre every potential rival to his throne." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

---

### v. 6 — "And when Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, he fell facedown in reverence. Then David said, 'Mephibosheth!' 'I am your servant,' he replied."

- **Mephibosheth's fear:** The Pulpit Commentary states: "Mephibosheth probably expected the fate which in the East usually befalls the members of a dethroned dynasty. Subsequently in Israel each new line of usurpers put to death every male relative of its predecessor… Looked at, then, in the light of Oriental policy, David's conduct was most generous." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **The name:** Ellicott notes his name is given as Merib-baal in 1 Chron. 8:34; 9:40 — the "baal" element was later changed to "bosheth" ("shame") after Jezebel's time when Baal became the title of the Phoenician sun god. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **David's affectionate address:** Gill says David spoke the name "with great vehemency and affection, as glad that he had found one of Jonathan's posterity." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/9.htm]

---

### v. 7 — "'Do not be afraid,' said David, 'for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.'"

- **"Do not fear":** Enduring Word says these words "would be cruel or meaningless unless David gave Mephibosheth a reason to not fear." David gives concrete reasons: restored lands and a permanent seat at his table. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

- **The land restoration:** The Pulpit Commentary notes David probably restored not only the lands at Gibeah but "Saul's estates generally." There was likely already "on Ziba's part a grudge against Mephibosheth for thus getting back from the king what he had hoped to keep as his own." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Eating at the king's table:** Gill calls this "a very great favour and high honour, and showed what an unshaken friendship he had for his father." It meant an apartment in the court and a permanent place as the king's guest. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Grace, not earned:** John MacArthur (GTY, Reformed Baptist) writes: "David not only made provision for Mephibosheth's physical and material needs, but in effect adopted him: 'Mephibosheth ate at David's table as one of the king's sons' (v. 11)." [https://www.gty.org/blogs/B160729/godly-compassion-for-hurting-people]

- **Covenant basis:** Ligonier notes that *hesed* "consists of more than a sentiment. It bears fruit in tangible action." David showed it by giving land and a seat at the table. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mephibosheth-sits-at-kings-table]

---

### v. 8 — "Mephibosheth bowed down and said, 'What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?'"

- **"Dead dog":** This was the most contemptible thing imaginable in the ancient Near East (cf. 2 Sam. 3:8; 16:9; 1 Sam. 24:14). Ellicott says Mephibosheth's "humility is more than oriental; it is abject, arising no doubt in part from his infirmity." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- The Pulpit Commentary offers a cultural nuance: "At first sight this extreme self-humiliation makes us look on Mephibosheth as a poor creature… But really this is to impose on an Oriental hyperbole a Western exactness of meaning." Mephibosheth meant to express great gratitude and acknowledge the disparity of rank, similar to David's own self-description to Saul (1 Sam. 24:14). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Spurgeon's devotional application:** "If Mephibosheth was thus humbled by David's kindness, what shall we be in the presence of our gracious Lord? The more grace we have, the less we shall think of ourselves, for grace, like light, reveals our impurity." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-9-commentary]

- Enduring Word: "Mephibosheth didn't feel worthy of such generosity. He considered himself a dead dog, meaning a worthless and insignificant person." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

---

### v. 9 — "Then the king summoned Saul's servant Ziba and said to him, 'I have given to your master's grandson all that belonged to Saul and to all his house.'"

- **"Master's son" (Hebrew):** The Pulpit Commentary notes that strictly Mephibosheth was Saul's grandson, but "words of relationship are used in a very general way in Hebrew." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Gill notes some take "thy master's son" to refer to Micha (Mephibosheth's son), but most understand it as Mephibosheth himself, the grandson of Saul whose servant Ziba had been. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/9.htm]

---

### v. 10 — "'You and your sons and servants are to work the ground for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master's grandson may have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master's grandson, is always to eat at my table.' Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants."

- **Food for the household:** Though Mephibosheth ate at the king's table, he had a household to maintain (wife, son, servants). The Pulpit Commentary explains: "'food to eat' includes everything necessary, as does our prayer for 'daily bread.' He would live at Jerusalem as a nobleman and Ziba would cultivate his estates, paying, as is usual in the East, a fixed proportion of the value of the produce." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Ellicott similarly says this is "to be taken in the general sense of means for the support of his household as a royal prince." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Ziba's wealth:** Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants — he "had evidently thriven; for, beginning as a slave in Saul's household, he had now several wives and many slaves of his own, and had become a person of considerable importance." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Dr. Constable notes: "David provided for Mephibosheth's needs in Jerusalem, but Ziba and his family cultivated Mephibosheth's land and brought the produce to David. Thus the produce of his land paid the cost of Mephibosheth's maintenance." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]

- Enduring Word: "In addition to the land, David gave Mephibosheth servants to work the land. The food from the land was for Mephibosheth's family, because he now ate at David's table." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

---

### v. 11 — "And Ziba said to the king, 'Your servant will do all that my lord the king has commanded.' So Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's own sons."

- **Textual issue:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew is difficult because it makes David say the same thing three times. "The text is probably corrupt… Of the many emendations proposed, the most probable is that of the LXX and Syriac, which make this clause an observation of the historian pointing out the high honour done to Mephibosheth in placing him on an equality with David's own sons." The reading would be: "So Mephibosheth ate at the king's table as one of the king's sons." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Ellicott agrees: "It is better to take them as a part of the narrative. In that case, David himself must have written this account, unless, with the LXX and Syriac, we read, 'at the table of David,' instead of 'my table.'" [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Gill also addresses the textual difficulty, noting that Abarbinel and others thought these were Ziba's words continued — but "the phrase 'my table' seems to be too arrogant for Ziba to say, and rather fits the mouth of David the king." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Like one of the king's sons:** This is the highest honour — adoption into the royal family. John MacArthur (GTY) calls it an effective adoption. [https://www.gty.org/blogs/B160729/godly-compassion-for-hurting-people]

---

### v. 12 — "And Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth."

- **Mica (Micha):** The Pulpit Commentary notes this son became the representative of the house of Saul and "had a numerous offspring, who were leading men in the tribe of Benjamin until the Captivity (see 1 Chron. 8:35–40; 9:40–44)." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

- Ellicott adds that as far as recorded, Mica was Mephibosheth's only child, but his posterity was numerous. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **The mention of Mica also helps date the chapter:** Mephibosheth was five at his father's death; now he has a young son, so perhaps 15–20 years have passed. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/9.htm]

---

### v. 13 — "So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table, and he was lame in both feet."

- **From hiding to the royal city:** Enduring Word: "No longer hiding in fear of the king, this descendant of Saul now lived openly among the people of God." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

- **The lameness remains:** This is a key theological point made by several traditions:
  - Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic): "Though David's grace restored Mephibosheth's status, wealth, and honor, it did not heal his lameness — a reminder that the King's favor changes how we see ourselves and our standing even when our weaknesses remain." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]
  - Spurgeon (Baptist): "Lameness is no bar to sonship; the cripple is as much the heir as if he could run like Asahel. Our right does not limp, though our might may. A king's table is a noble hiding-place for lame legs, and at the gospel feast we learn to glory in infirmities, because the power of Christ resteth upon us." [https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/morneve/morneve.d0527am.html]
  - Spurgeon also notes the practical consequence: Mephibosheth's lameness meant "he could not go up with the king when he fled from the city, and was therefore maligned and injured by his servant Ziba." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary]

- **Repeated mention of lameness:** Ellicott says this fact is repeated "on account of its bearing upon the narrative in 2 Sam. 16:1–4; 19:24–30." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/9.htm]

- **Literary-critical perspective (noted in Constable):** Some modern scholars (Sternberg, Ackerman, Perdue) raise the question of mixed motives — given David's loathing of "the lame and the blind" since the Jebusite war (2 Sam. 5:6–8), was David keeping Mephibosheth close partly to keep an eye on the last of Saul's line? Constable notes this view but does not endorse it. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]

---

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

The search and fetch limits prevented me from retrieving dedicated pages from several traditions. Based on what was found:

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises *hesed* as covenant love that must bear fruit in tangible action, and draws the parallel to Christ's greater *hesed* in dying for His enemies. Also stresses that we must show such love particularly to "the orphan, the widow, and others who may be unable to repay our kindness." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mephibosheth-sits-at-kings-table]

- **Baptist / Reformed Baptist (Spurgeon, GTY/ MacArthur, Desiring God/Piper):** Spurgeon draws a rich Gospel typology — the Father receives us at His table because He sees in our faces the features of His beloved Jesus. MacArthur emphasises David's adoption of Mephibosheth as a picture of divine compassion. Piper (Desiring God) notes David's gentleness and "kindness of God" as a striking pattern in his life despite his flaws. [https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/morneve/morneve.d0527am.html], [https://www.gty.org/blogs/B160729/godly-compassion-for-hurting-people], [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/man-of-war-and-grace]

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strong emphasis on the story as a picture of unexpected grace, the initiative of the King, and the fact that grace does not remove all weakness but changes status and standing. Guzik also draws the application that believers are called to be like David — seeking out the poor, weak, and hidden to bless them. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-9/]

- **Evangelical (Precept Austin, Constable):** Heavy focus on covenant loyalty (*hesed*) and typology (David as a type of Christ, Mephibosheth as a type of the sinner). Constable also notes the political dimension — David's kindness to Saul's house helped secure Benjamite loyalty. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2samuel_9_commentary], [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-9.html]
